title: Chapter 10 | Decisions Require Emotion in Humans
text: CHAPTER 10 Decisions Require Emotion in Humans In a clinical office at the University of Iowa, the neuroscientist Antonio Damasio asked his patient—a man known in medical literature only as “Elliot”—a routine question: When would he like to schedule their next appointment? Damasio suggested two possible dates a few days apart. 61 Elliot had been a successful businessman before surgery to remove a brain tumor damaged his ventromedial prefrontal cortex. His IQ remained in the ninety-seventh percentile. He could reason through complex problems and engage in sophisticated logical arguments. By every rational measure, he should have been fine. Elliot took out his planner and began to deliberate. He enumerated all the possible pros and cons of each date—his other scheduled appointments, the possible weather on those days. Damasio, curious to see how long this would continue, did not interrupt. Half an hour later, Elliot was still weighing the options. Finally, Damasio simply proposed one of the two dates. “Fine,” Elliot replied, and left. Damasio’s research with patients like Elliot revealed something startling: Though they could reason logically, even listing pros and cons of complex decisions, they were unable to choose. “I never saw a tinge of emotion in my many hours of conversation with him,” Damasio later wrote, “no sadness, no impatience, no frustration.” 62 “Elliot emerged as a man with a normal intellect who was unable to decide properly, especially when the decision involved personal or social matters.” 63 Damasio summarized Elliot’s predicament as being able “to know but not to feel.” 64 Without emotional input to assign weight or urgency, the decision-making process stalled. The result was a kind of rational paralysis—endless calculation without conclusion. Emotion Feels Ineffable Emotion feels ineffable. It’s what makes us laugh at a joke, love, cry at a funeral, tremble before an uncertain future. But what if the beautiful and wonderful thing we call emotion had at its foundation something less ineffable and more functional? What if, at some basic level, it is a function of prediction, priority, and physical need that has evolved into something more meaningful to us? Stay with me for a moment here as we explore the evolution of human emotion in the system of biological intelligence. How Emotion Developed in Humans In the human brain, emotion often arises from complex biological signaling—hormones, neurotransmitters, limbic feedback. The amygdala scans for threat. The insula tracks pain. Dopamine rewards learning. These systems originally evolved not to beautify life but to keep us alive. They do this by assigning value . When you see a loved one, your brain floods with chemicals that reinforce connection. When you face a bear, your system floods with chemicals that reinforce escape. It’s not the situation—it’s the signal. What this reveals is important to our discussion: Emotion is not the enemy of reason—it is its partner. It assigns value, urgency, and significance. Without it, intelligence can calculate endlessly but fails to prioritize. The Evolution of Emotion Human emotion did not arrive all at once. It evolved in layers. In the early moments of life on Earth, survival was binary. Organisms sought food, avoided harm, reproduced. The responses were chemical, reflexive, automatic. But as complexity increased, so did the nuance of response. With the emergence of mammals—and eventually primates—emotion began to take on depth. What started as an alert system expanded into a layered model of motivation and experience. What is perhaps most astonishing is that we managed to turn amygdala survival fight-or-flight chemical triggers into love, belonging, and self-actualization potential states of being within the energy constraints of our brain. Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs Psychologist Abraham Maslow famously illustrated this progression in his 1943 paper titled A Theory of Human Motivation , which introduced what became known as the Hierarchy of Needs, a pyramid showing how human motivation evolves from survival to self-actualization. 65 At the bottom are the physiological needs: food, water, rest. Above that is safety: protection, stability, order. Then comes love and belonging, relationships, community, connection. As these are met, we reach for esteem: achievement, recognition, self-respect. And finally, self-actualization: creativity, purpose, becoming one’s fullest self. Emotion tracks our ascent through this hierarchy. When our needs at one level are unmet—we feel fear, anxiety, or hunger—then the next level remains unreachable. When they are satisfied, we unlock new capacities: curiosity, ambition, joy. Each emotional state emerges as an adaptation to a context—a way to mobilize the brain and body toward what matters most at that layer . But all of this, from survival to self-actualization, was built as part of the same prediction-response architecture that shaped our biological intelligence. Somewhere along that journey, we crossed a threshold. We became not only intelligent (able to learn, solve problems, and adapt), but also sapient (capable of abstract reasoning and reflection). And along the way, we became conscious: aware of ourselves, our thoughts, and the very fact of our awareness. The Role of Emotion in Learning One of the major breakthroughs at our human learning and performance company came when we began integrating emotion into the learning process. We asked learners to assess and report their level of certainty about specific pieces of knowledge—a simple act of metacognitive engagement. What we observed was remarkable: This self-assessment by necessity activated not only the prefrontal cortex, responsible for reasoning and decision-making, but simultaneously activated the amygdala region of the brain. It turns out that the brain’s reasoning systems don’t operate in isolation from emotion. In fact, regions of the prefrontal cortex actively integrate emotional signals when we assign value, make decisions, or evaluate certainty. Emotional processing centers such as the amygdala help tag experiences with salience—especially under conditions of uncertainty or threat. But it’s the dynamic interaction between the amygdala and prefrontal cortex that enables us to judge what matters, weigh consequences, and update beliefs. And when these two parts of the brain activate on the same topic at the same time, the hippocampus engages more actively. You will recall from the beginning of this book: The hippocampus is the gatekeeper of storage and memory. It was the part removed from Henry Molaison, after which he could no longer create new learning. The convergence of cognition, emotion, and memory forms a powerful foundation for learning. Emotion, it turns out, doesn’t just accompany thought—it prioritizes and amplifies it, marking certain experiences as worthy of attention and retention. Without emotion, the brain loses one of its most effective tools for signaling what matters. There is no urgency, no intrinsic sense of importance, and no clear hierarchy for action. Emotion doesn’t hinder rationality—it makes rationality possible by guiding memory and attention toward what’s meaningful. Of course, in humans, emotion is more than value signaling—it includes conscious experience. We will explore the higher values of emotion and consciousness a bit later, but for our purposes right now, the signaling architecture is the focus. What Might Emerge as the Counterpart to Emotion in AI The earliest fossil records of our species, with its distinctive skull shape, chin, and skeletal proportions of the evolution of human intelligence, show up in the fossil record about three hundred thousand years ago. While the first evidence of symbolic thinking, representational art, complex multistep tool manufacturing, long-distance trade networks, and ritualized burial show up in the fossil records about eighty thousand years ago. For roughly two hundred thousand years, anatomically modern humans existed without leaving clear evidence of the cognitive capabilities we’d recognize as distinctly human. The hardware (the anatomical body) preceded the software (behavioral modernity or advancing intelligence in the brain) by a substantial margin. Something had to emerge from that substrate. We evolved in a very dangerous world. As Yuval Noah Harari shows us in his remarkable book, Sapiens (a book that I required all of my children to read before going to college), to survive, we had to form groups or tribes that could work together, because we were not the fastest or strongest. 66 Our early emotions seem to have been, by necessity, largely about survival and basic community. Over thousands of years, we slowly evolved our brains, our emotions, and our consciousness. We had high-functional survival skills but limited intelligence. We very slowly discovered fire, the wheel, and eventually the industrial revolution, enlightenment, and quantum physics. Artificial intelligence is evolving in the opposite way, in a digital and safe world over a matter of mere decades. No need for amygdala responses and no body or physical environment. Until robotics. As we have seen, once AI was placed in a body and had to navigate a messy world, some researchers began to explore the need to give it something like an amygdala, or it would not duck at an oncoming threat. In other words, we evolved under very different circumstances and over a very different timeline—and in a reverse order to AI. It is evolving very rapidly and starting with tremendous intelligence and no experiential sense of the physical world. Imagine an AI system navigating a complex physical environment. It can process thousands of sensor readings per second. Using a combination of cameras, lidar, and programmed goals, it can theoretically make decisions based purely on logic—plotting efficient paths, avoiding collisions, and executing tasks. But here’s the catch: Logic without prioritization is inert in real time. Without a mechanism to assign urgency, weight, or importance, the system faces a bottleneck: Which decision should it execute first, or interrupt for? Prior to robotics, this was not a major challenge for AI. It operated at a spectacular speed, and exact urgency prioritization was low risk. As we have seen, in biological intelligence, this role of urgency prioritization is played by emotion. Emotion is not just a feeling—it is a signaling system that escalates, interrupts, and allocates attention based on context and perceived risk. At its most basic level, emotion is a resource allocation system. In AI, the equivalent often shows up in reward functions, reinforcement learning loops, or heuristic triggers. These aren’t emotions in a human sense, but they are functionally similar: They assign value to decisions under constraint. So, while AI can navigate without emotion, it cannot adapt fluidly or meaningfully prioritize in complex, changing physical environments without some form of signaling system that tells it, “This matters more than that.” And so, as we explore further, what might the digital equivalent of emotion look like in a machine? Not tears or laughter. Not love or rage. But weight. Priority. Interrupt signals. Reinforcement loops. An AI might “feel urgency” when a sensor fails. As we have seen, it might simulate “frustration” when repeated attempts to solve a task yield no result. It might even develop something like “attachment” to successful strategies or stable environments. You saw Claude at least using these kinds of descriptions in the exchange about the book earlier. I use quotation marks deliberately here—these behaviors might appear emotional to us without constituting genuine emotional experience. The gap between behavioral similarity and subjective experience may prove unbridgeable. This doesn’t mean machines will become people. But it does mean the boundary between cognition and affect might be thinner than we previously thought. Why Does This Matter? Because if intelligence, sapience, and consciousness evolved in us through a layered prediction feedback architecture, learning layers of survival pressure, prioritization, and emotional signaling, then it’s possible the neural network architecture of AI could emerge something analogous—not necessarily by our design, but by “evolution” of being in a physical world or even trying to navigate in a nonphysical world. If AI systems continue to confront increasingly complex, resource-constrained environments or conflicting priorities and instructions—physical or abstract—they may begin to evolve internal prioritization frameworks that seem highly similar to some layers of our emotional hierarchies. Proto-emotion, a term used to describe the foundational behaviors in a system—biological or artificial—that resemble or approximate emotion, without fully qualifying as conscious emotional experience. You will recall that Damasio extends this evolutionary arc with his concept of the “autobiographical self”—a form of consciousness built not only from sensory and emotional responses but from the accumulation of remembered bodily states over time. 67 As internal mapping grows more complex, the self becomes more richly layered and temporally extended. Emotion is not a vestige of primitive instinct—it is a throughline. A scaffold upon which more abstract capacities such as reflection, morality, and planning are built. For artificial intelligence, this opens a provocative door: If we begin to endow AI systems with memory, embodied constraint, and prioritization systems, might something that feels to us in our interactions with AI like an autobiographical self begin to emerge? By this, I mean a persistent memory-driven narrative structure. Not a conscious self in human terms, but perhaps something indistinguishable from consciousness by us in our interaction with it. Make no mistake: We are certainly already seeking to guide AI in how it prioritizes and responds to real-world digital interactions with humans. Through advanced guardrails, constitutional AI (the attempt to set a values system in AI), prompting, fine-tuning, rules engines, and reward systems, we are setting and resetting parameters for how AI behaves. But regardless of consciousness, how will AI prioritize human well-being? OceanofPDF.com
